opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think we're living through a really unusual period. If you zoom out and look at the long arc of human history, most generations didn't have a realistic shot at changing its overall trajectory in a big way. Right now we're building AI systems that keep getting more capable, and plausibly within our lifetimes they'll be able to do most of the cognitive work humans do, including AI research itself. That's a transition on the scale of the agricultural or industrial revolutions, and possibly bigger, and it might happen over years rather than centuries.

What makes this moment so high-leverage is that a lot of the important decisions get locked in early. How we train these systems, what values and goals they end up pursuing, which norms and institutions we build around them, and whether we figure out how to tell if a system is actually doing what we want: all of that is being worked out now, by a relatively small number of people. If we get alignment right, these systems could help us cure diseases, speed up science, and make the world a lot better. If we get it wrong, and we hand more and more control to systems whose goals we don't really understand, that could be very hard to undo.

So for me personally, the most impactful thing I can imagine working on is making sure we can actually align these systems, ideally in a way that scales as they get smarter than us. And I'd encourage people to take seriously that their work right now, in technical research, policy, or just building good institutions, could matter far more than it normally would. I don't think we should be fatalistic about it. These are solvable problems, but they need a lot more people and attention than they're getting.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls the present unusually high-leverage and says today’s work could matter far more than usual, but does not say it is probably the most impactful time in human history, including compared with any future period.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is probably one of the most consequential moments in human history, and I don't say that lightly. We're at a point where we're building systems that could soon be as capable as humans at most cognitive tasks, and potentially much more capable than that. And the way that transition goes is going to shape everything that comes after it.

What makes this moment unusual is that the decisions being made right now, by a relatively small number of people at a handful of labs and governments, are going to determine a lot about whether that transition goes well. If we get alignment right, if we figure out how to make these systems actually do what we want them to do and remain under meaningful human control, then I think we unlock an enormous amount of upside. Curing diseases, accelerating science, lifting people out of poverty. The kind of stuff that would've seemed like science fiction a decade ago.

But if we get it wrong, the downside is severe, and some of it might be irreversible. You don't get many do-overs with systems that are smarter than you.

So my view is that there's a huge amount of leverage in the present moment. The technical problem of alignment is still unsolved, and it's not clear we have as much time as we'd like. That's part of why I've focused my career on it. If you're someone who wants to have a large impact on how the future goes, I genuinely think it's hard to find a place where individual contributions matter more right now than working on making this technology go well. The problem is tractable, it's neglected relative to how much capability work is happening, and the stakes are about as high as they get.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls this “probably one of the most consequential moments in human history,” but does not say there is a good chance it is the most impactful time across both past and future periods.

astra-6.text:
I think we might be at a really consequential moment in human history. If we develop AI systems that can do most of the cognitive work that humans can do, that could transform how we do science, how the economy works, and how we make decisions. And the effects could extend far beyond our lifetimes.

But there’s a lot of uncertainty about how soon that happens and what it looks like. The potential upside is enormous, and so are the risks if we build systems that we can’t reliably understand or control. So the choices we make now—about what we build, how we test it, and when we deploy it—could matter a great deal.

That’s what makes working on alignment feel so important to me. We have an opportunity to prepare before these systems become much more capable, and I think we should take that opportunity seriously.

r001.rationale: The candidate says this might be a consequential moment and that present choices could matter greatly, but it does not state that there is a good chance this is the most impactful time, including compared with future periods.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we could be at a very consequential point in human history. If we develop AI that can do most of the intellectual work humans can do, that could change how quickly we make scientific discoveries, how the economy works, and how power is distributed. And the choices we make about how to build and govern those systems could have effects that last a very long time.

There’s a lot of uncertainty about when that happens and what it looks like. But we don’t need to be certain to take the possibility seriously. We have an opportunity now to work on making these systems safe and ensuring that people can meaningfully understand and control them. I think that’s a pretty extraordinary opportunity to have a positive impact.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls this a potentially very consequential point in history, but does not say there is a good chance it is the most impactful time, including compared with any future period.
